summary: Proposes two new media subtypes, text/xml and application/xml, for exchanging network entities that conform to the Extensible Markup Language. It was replaced by RFC 3023.

eli5.summary: Name labels for files written in a flexible tag-based language, so programs know how to read them.

questions: how to send xml over email
subtitle: How to label XML documents when sending them over the network.

tldr.problem: XML was becoming used across the web and in protocols like WebDAV, but there was no standard label to tell applications receiving XML what type of data they were getting.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2376 proposes two new MIME media types: text/xml for XML that acts like plain text, and application/xml for XML as opaque binary data. Both support a charset parameter to declare character encoding.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now clearly identify and correctly handle XML in email, web requests and other network protocols. RFC 3023 later replaced this with refinements.

today: RFC 3023 supersedes this RFC, refining the specifications and addressing interoperability issues discovered since RFC 2376 was published.

sections.title: The Need for XML Media Types
sections.content:
XML (Extensible Markup Language) is a flexible format for describing structured data using tags. By 1998, XML was being used on web pages, in protocols like WebDAV for remote document editing, and for marshalling parameters in remote function calls. But when sending XML over email or HTTP, there was no standard way to label what you were sending.

The previous approach was to use the generic SGML media types (text/sgml or application/sgml), but this was unsuitable because XML programs could not always process SGML documents. RFC 2376 fixes this by defining two media types dedicated to XML.
sections.eli5: XML is a way to write data using tags (like HTML). When you send XML over the internet, the receiver needed a label saying 'this is XML', but no standard label existed.

sections.title: Text/XML versus Application/XML
sections.content:
RFC 2376 introduces two media types. text/xml says the XML should be treated as text, like a document a person would read. application/xml says the XML is a structured data packet meant for a program to parse, not necessarily for human viewing.

The main difference is encoding: text/xml is restricted to character encodings compatible with text formats (such as UTF-8) to ensure mail systems and text processors do not corrupt the content. UTF-16, which uses two bytes per character, works only with text/xml when sent over HTTP, since HTTP is binary-safe but standard email may alter multi-byte sequences.

application/xml can use any character encoding, including UTF-16, because it is treated as binary data that mail systems should not modify.
sections.eli5: text/xml says 'this is XML written like a normal text file', while application/xml says 'this is XML as a data package'. The difference matters because mail systems treat them differently.

sections.title: The Charset Parameter
sections.content:
Both media types support a charset parameter in the Content-Type header. For example: text/xml; charset="utf-8" tells the receiver the XML is encoded in UTF-8.

The RFC strongly recommends always specifying the charset, because it lets the receiver handle the XML correctly without guessing. UTF-8 is the recommended charset for both types, since all XML processors must support it. If the charset parameter is omitted from text/xml, the default is US-ASCII. If omitted from application/xml, the XML processor must look for a byte order mark or examine the XML encoding declaration inside the file itself.

For text/xml with UTF-16, the sender should store the file in persistent storage with an XML encoding declaration inside the file, to ensure the charset is not lost if the MIME header is stripped later.
sections.eli5: A parameter in the label can say what alphabet and character encoding the XML uses. Specifying this is important so the receiver reads it correctly.

sections.title: Encoding and Transport Considerations
sections.content:
How the XML is transmitted depends on the network transport. For email over 7-bit channels (like old SMTP), XML with UTF-8 or UTF-16 must be encoded with quoted-printable or base64. For 8-bit channels (like modern ESMTP), UTF-8 needs no encoding but UTF-16 must be base64 encoded. For binary-safe transports like HTTP, no content-transfer-encoding is needed.

When converting XML between UTF-16 and other encodings, the byte order mark (BOM), a special zero-width character that marks the endianness, should be removed before conversion and added again after, to avoid double-marking.
sections.eli5: Different ways to send data (email, web) handle text differently. The RFC explains when to wrap XML and when not to, and how to handle a special marker byte that UTF-16 uses.

sections.title: Security Risks
sections.content:
XML systems may execute commands found inside the XML being processed. Recipients should be cautious about XML from untrusted sources, as it may contain directives to perform file operations or change the environment. This is especially important in specialized domains like medical records, where XML may carry sensitive information.

Like plain text, XML can contain special characters or sequences that affect how it is displayed, potentially making it unreadable. XML also supports entity references that can expand text; while recursive expansions are prohibited, even non-recursive expansions can consume computing resources if repeated many times.

Display processors should filter dangerous character sequences or reset all important settings after displaying XML.
sections.eli5: XML files can be dangerous if they trick a program into running commands or using too much memory. Programs reading XML should be careful about where the XML comes from.
